question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

5.text:
Trisyllabic laxing is the English shortening/laxing of a stressed vowel that is
followed by two light syllables, e.g.

derive /dɪˈraɪv/  >  derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/
serene /səˈriːn/  >  serenity /səˈrɛ.nə.ti/
grateful /ˈɡreɪt.fəl/ > gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/

i.e. /aɪ/ → /ɪ/, /iː/ → /ɛ/, /eɪ/ → /æ/ etc. in a word of ≥3 syllables
with the stress staying on the same morphemic syllable as in the base.

* derivative, serenity and gratitude are all morphologically complex
polysyllabic forms and the stressed vowel of the base is laxed in the
derived form in the normal trisyllabic way.

* pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/ and shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ are disyllabic.  The
/iː/ → /ɛ/ of please > pleasant and the /eɪ/ → /æ/ of shade > shadow are
vowel shortening / pre-fortis clipping in a disyllabic environment and
not the classic penultimate/antepenultimate trisyllabic laxation.

The clearest non-example in the set is southern.  southern is
disyllabic /ˈsʌð.ən/ < south /saʊθ/ + -ern.  The change /aʊ/ → /ʌ/ is a
regular development of south-ern and is not the /iː,uː,eɪ,oʊ/ → /ɪ,ʊ,ɛ,ɔ/
trisyllabic laxing that is shown by derivative, serenity and gratitude.
Shadow, and to a lesser extent pleasant, are in the same disyllabic
class.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow is the clear non-case. 

southern /ˈsʌðən/, pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ and shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ are
bi-syllabic in Present-Day English and can therefore never be the
environment for a historical trisyllabic shortening/laxing.  In fact
shadow is the only genuinely native Germanic item in the set and it
never acquires a third syllable at all.

The three Latinate items that are trisyllabic or more in P.D.E. are
the textbook cases of the Middle-English trisyllabic shortening/laxing
that turns a long/stressed vowel of the disyllabic base lax/short when
a further unstressed syllable is added.

* serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ < *seren-e  /səˈriːn/ :  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/ < *grate /greɪt/ :  the stressed vowel is
shortened/laxed in the trisyllabic derivative
* derivative /dɪˈrɪvə­tɪv/ < derive /dɪˈraɪv/ :  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/ in the
stressed second syllable of the four-syllable derivative.

Southern and pleasant are also bi-syllabic and so do not instantiate
the process in the normal synchronic sense; shadow is the canonical
native bi-syllabic control.

The classic environment for trisyllabic laxing is a long stressed vowel in a disyllabic base that is lengthened to three or more syllables by suffixation, e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvə­tɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate-/grateful /ˈɡreɪtfl/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

All of those are genuine trisyllabic/ polysyllabic formations with a stem vowel that is laxed under the trisyllabic condition. 

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is a native Germanic inheritance, OE sceadu, with no suffixal lengthening of a long-vowel base into a trisyllabic shape and no stem-vowel laxing of the trisyllabic type.

Shadow is the most unequivocally non-trisyllabic-laxt item in the set.

In the productive English pattern the tense vowel of a base is shortened/laxed
when the base is extended by a suffix so that the stressed syllable is followed
by two or more weak syllables, e.g. 

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ → derivative /dɪˈrɪvəˌtɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ → serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ → pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /greɪt/ ~ grateful /ˈgreɪtfəl/ → gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/
  /eɪ/ > /æ/
* south /saʊθ/ → souther[n] /ˈsʌð(ə)n/ AmE  /aʊ/ > /ʌ/

All of them are the regular tense → lax alternation that is normally
described as trisyllabic / post-stress laxing, even if the modern surface
form is disyllabic in the case of *pleasant* and *southern*.

*shadow* is not a trisyllabic laxing derivative at all. 
*shade* /ʃeɪd/ → *shadow* /ˈʃædoʊ/ shows the regular Old English /a/
development and the Anglo-Norman *a*-spelling before /w/ that gives
/æ/ in the modern form, and the word remains disyllabic with no
suffixal extension of the stressed syllable creating the
tense/lax alternation that defines the trisyllabic laxing class. It is
the only item in the set that does not instantiate the productive
*BASE Vs → BASE-suffix V-lax* alternation. 

That is the normal textbook odd one out; by strict syllable count the
disyllabic modern forms *southern* and *pleasant* are of course not
trisyllabic today, the classic three-syllable cases being *gratitude*,
*derivative* and *serenity*.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which item has not undergone the historical tense→lax shortening/laxing that occurs when a stressed long/tense vowel is followed by two weak syllables in a derived form.

Evidence collected in round 0:
* Core diagnostic given by colleagues: base with tense/long vowel → suffixed derivative with same stress but lax/short vowel, e.g. derive /dɪˈraɪv/ → derivative /dɪˈrɪvəˌtɪv/ /aɪ/>/ɪ/; serene /səˈriːn/ → serenity /səˈrɛnəti/ /iː/>/ɛ/; grate/grateful → gratitude /eɪ/>/æ/; please → pleasant /iː/>/ɛ/; south → southern /aʊ/>/ʌ/ in AmE /ˈsʌðən/.

* derivative, serenity and gratitude are consistently identified as textbook polysyllabic trisyllabic-laxing cases with the stressed vowel laxed under suffixation.

* shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is uniformly described as the non-case: OE sceadu, native Germanic inheritance, /æ/ is inherited short vowel, no suffixal extension of a long-vowel base and no BASE → BASE-suffix tense/lax alternation. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,6,7 explicitly nominate shadow as the odd one out.

Disagreement noted:
* Colleague 1,4,7 treat southern and pleasant as still showing the regular tense→lax alternation even though the modern surface forms are disyllabic.
* Colleagues 2,3 argue synchronically southern /ˈsʌðən/ and pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ are bi-syllabic and therefore never enter a trisyllabic environment; their vowel changes are described as disyllabic shortening/anglicisation rather than classic trisyllabic laxing.
